periods.analysis: We are starting this sequence at 82% of the annual affordable-units delivery target, which keeps Harborview in yellow: close enough to be recoverable, but not yet where Council asked us to be. The main story is timing, not lack of pipeline; the East Wharf 96-unit closing, the Cedar & 12th inclusionary set-aside, and two airport-corridor LIHTC projects are all active, but several certificates of occupancy landed just outside the quarter reporting window. I’m comfortable that the Housing, Planning, and Finance teams have the right projects on the board, and I want us to be equally disciplined about the data cutoffs so departments get credit when units are truly deliverable.
periods.recommendations: Keep the weekly Affordable Delivery Tracker current every Friday by noon, with Planning confirming permit status and Housing confirming affordability covenants. Assign a single closeout owner for East Wharf and Cedar & 12th so any inspection, utility-release, or covenant-recording issue is cleared within five business days. For Council reporting, keep the yellow status and note the specific watch-item: units that are built but not yet counted because final documentation is pending.

periods.analysis: The measure moved from 82% to 78%, a decrease of 4 points, so we stayed yellow and lost a little ground at the exact moment everyone was hoping for year-end lift. The drop is mostly a reporting and delivery-sequencing issue: Harborview Landing Phase 2 had elevator acceptance rescheduled, and the Bayline Apartments covenant package needed one more lender signature before units could be booked. That said, yellow means we should be watchful, not defensive; residents do not experience a unit as delivered until it is permitted, inspected, covenanted, and ready for occupancy. I appreciate the departments keeping the facts clean here, even when the clean answer is less flattering than the press release timeline.
periods.recommendations: Run a January closeout huddle with Housing, Building Safety, Legal, and the Harborview Housing Trust to separate true slippage from documentation lag. Create a two-column Council appendix: units physically complete and units formally countable, so the 78% result is transparent and credible. Sustain the projects that are moving well by fast-tracking final inspections for small infill sites under 20 units on the Tuesday/Thursday affordable-housing inspection route.

periods.analysis: This quarter the measure fell from 78% to 73%, down 5 points, which moves us into red because we are now below the 75% threshold. I am concerned, and I also want to be precise: the problem is not that Harborview stopped producing affordable housing, it is that too many units are sitting in the last mile between financing, permits, and occupancy. The clearest pain points are the Northgate Station 72-unit file waiting on stormwater revisions, the Seaport Commons resubmittal after flood-elevation comments, and delayed draw documentation on two Housing Trust gap-financing awards. Red is the right status because the annual target is slipping, but this is a managed red with named projects, named blockers, and owners who can move them.
periods.recommendations: Stand up a 30-day Affordable Units Recovery Sprint chaired by Housing with Planning, Building Safety, Public Works, and Legal at the table every Monday. Put Northgate Station, Seaport Commons, and the two Housing Trust awards on a red-project list with one accountable blocker, one next action, and one date for each. Brief Council that the value is 73%, down 5 points, and that staff will return next quarter with project-level movement rather than general assurances.

periods.analysis: We improved from 73% to 78%, up 5 points, which moves the measure back from red to yellow. That is the kind of recovery I like to see: not dramatic storytelling, just disciplined follow-through on the Q1 blocker list. Northgate Station cleared stormwater on the second resubmittal, the Seaport Commons flood-elevation comments were resolved through revised first-floor mechanical placement, and Building Safety added a dedicated Wednesday morning inspection block for affordable-housing closeouts. We are still short of the 100% target, so yellow remains appropriate, but the quarter-over-quarter movement shows the recovery sprint is working.
periods.recommendations: Keep the Recovery Sprint in place for one more quarter, but narrow it to projects within 60 days of certificate of occupancy or covenant recording. Extend the Wednesday inspection block through September and publish the eligible project list so developers know how to use it. Watch the next risk item closely: utility-release timing for the airport-corridor projects, especially where transformer procurement is being handled by the developer’s vendor.

periods.analysis: The measure rose from 78% to 86%, an 8-point gain, and that is the strongest improvement in this run so far while still remaining yellow. The gain reflects actual delivered units, not just better counting: Northgate Station units were booked, the first tranche at Harborview Landing Phase 2 cleared occupancy, and the Magnolia Court rehab cohort moved from temporary relocation back into restricted affordable units. This is good progress for a fast-growing coastal city where land, labor, insurance, and flood-resilience requirements all add friction to the housing pipeline. I do not want us to celebrate yellow as success, but I do want to recognize that the teams turned a red quarter into a credible upward arc.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the weekly tracker and Wednesday inspection block because they are producing visible results. Extend the recovery model upstream by adding a 90-day pre-close checklist for projects with public subsidy, including covenant drafts, utility releases, elevator testing, and floodplain documentation. For Council, frame 86% as momentum with a watch-item: Q4 depends on whether Harborview Landing Phase 2 and Bayline Apartments finish cleanly before the reporting cutoff.

periods.analysis: We moved from 86% to 78%, down 8 points, so the measure remains yellow but the year-end slide is real. The biggest issue was that expected Q4 deliveries did not all convert into countable affordable units: Bayline Apartments received partial occupancy, but the restricted-unit schedule was not fully recorded, and Harborview Landing Phase 2 held back a wing pending fire-alarm acceptance. Seasonal inspection compression also mattered, with holiday staffing and weather-related rechecks on coastal sites slowing closeout during the last two weeks of December. This is exactly why I keep nudging for deadline-aware reporting; we need to help departments look good by making the operational clock visible earlier, not by explaining it after the fact.
periods.recommendations: Begin Q1 with a dated carryover list for every Q4 unit not counted, including Bayline’s recorded-unit schedule and Harborview Landing’s fire-alarm acceptance. Require projects seeking year-end countability to have covenant documents substantially complete by November 15 and final inspection requests submitted by December 3) Keep the yellow status and identify the watch-item plainly: late-quarter documentation and life-safety acceptance are still too vulnerable to calendar pressure.

periods.analysis: The measure fell from 78% to 73%, a 5-point decrease, which puts us back in red for the second time in this chronology. I am concerned because the pattern is now visible: Harborview can recover during active management cycles, but we are still losing units when carryover projects hit financing amendments, inspections, or covenant recording at the same time. Bayline’s restricted-unit schedule was corrected, but several replacement units at the Spruce Street preservation portfolio were delayed when the contractor found balcony waterproofing failures, and the Seaport East permit set paused for a revised floodproofing detail. This is a managed red, but it is still red, and the annual target will not be met by optimism or end-of-quarter heroics.
periods.recommendations: Reopen the red-project cadence immediately, with a two-week executive review for Bayline closeout, Spruce Street repairs, and Seaport East permitting. Add a Housing Delivery Risk Flag in ClearPoint for any project with more than 25 affordable units and a dependency on utility release, floodplain approval, or recorded covenant amendment. Ask Finance to pre-check subsidy disbursement conditions before construction closeout so completed units are not waiting on paperwork after inspection.

periods.analysis: We improved from 73% to 79%, up 6 points, moving the measure out of red and back into yellow. That is meaningful progress, especially because it came from the specific fixes named last quarter: Bayline’s schedule was recorded, Spruce Street reopened the first repaired buildings, and Seaport East cleared its revised floodproofing detail after the joint Planning-Public Works review. We are not at the 100% target, and at 79% we are still closer to the yellow threshold than I’d like, but the quarter shows that Harborview’s delivery system responds when the blockers are visible and owned. The arc over eight quarters is clear: the pipeline is real, the city is financially and operationally capable, and the last-mile discipline has to become standard practice rather than a rescue effort.
periods.recommendations: Keep the red-project cadence as a standing yellow-risk meeting through Q3, but limit attendance to owners with projects inside the next 120 days. Sustain the successful ClearPoint risk flag and require departments to update it before the monthly Council performance packet closes. Extend the inspection and covenant pre-check process to all Housing Trust-funded projects so the next improvement comes from routine execution, not another recovery sprint.

periods.analysis: Delivery is 102.1% of the annual target, down from 104.3% but still above 100%. This favorable output sits alongside worsening rent burden and delayed trust-fund loan closings.
periods.recommendations: Reconcile completed units and their component categories before publication, and distinguish delivered homes from awarded projects awaiting closing.
